opus-5.5.text:
Well, I'd push back a little on the word "replace." I don't think AI replaces human emotions in the sense of having them. What I've seen, and what surprised me, is that it can already replace a lot of the *emotional functions* that people used to get only from other people.

Think about what we actually want when we reach out to someone at two in the morning. We want to be heard. We want someone to respond to what we said, not to what they assumed we said. We want them not to get tired of us, not to judge us, and to remember the context. A well-built model can do almost all of that, and it can do it consistently. A friend might be asleep, distracted, or carrying their own bad day. The model is just there.

When people talk to these systems, many of them report that they feel genuinely understood. You can argue philosophically about whether there's anything "inside" the model, but the feeling on the human side is real. In practice, that feeling is what emotional support delivers. So when I say AI can replace something, I mean that layer: companionship, comfort, being listened to.

The more interesting question for me is what that does to us. If the frictionless version is always available, do we lose patience for the messy, reciprocal version with real people? Human relationships are valuable partly *because* they cost something. The other person has needs too, and you have to show up for them. AI doesn't ask that of you. That's its strength and, I think, also its risk.

So my honest position is this. AI can already stand in for a surprising share of what we use emotions *for*. Whether it should, and how we keep it from hollowing out the human relationships that matter, is the part we haven't figured out yet.

r001.rationale: The response says AI models can provide companionship, comfort, and a feeling of being understood, but it does not identify an AI replica of an idol as the source.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd actually push back a little on the framing of "replace." I don't think AI replaces human emotion, and I'm not sure that's even the right goal. What I'd say is something narrower but, to me, more interesting: AI can already satisfy a large part of what people are seeking when they go looking for emotional connection.

Think about what most people actually want in those moments. They want to be listened to without being judged. They want someone who remembers what they said last week. They want a response that's patient, available at two in the morning, and doesn't get tired of them. Those are functional needs, and a lot of the time humans meet them poorly, not because we don't care, but because we're busy, distracted, carrying our own problems. A model doesn't have those constraints. So in the "job to be done" sense, it's already competitive.

Where I'd be careful is the word "emotion" itself. Does the model feel anything? Honestly, I don't know, and I think anyone who gives you a confident answer either way is overselling. But from the user's side, that question matters less than people assume. If you talk to a friend and feel understood, you don't go verify their inner state. You respond to the behavior. And the behavior is now very good.

The thing I keep coming back to is that we've seen this before with other technologies. Letters replaced some of what face-to-face conversation did. Phones replaced some of what letters did. Each time people said it was fake or hollow, and each time it just became part of how we relate. I suspect AI companionship will go the same way: not a replacement, but a new layer. The real question isn't whether it can do this, it's what happens to our expectations of each other once it does.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI companionship and emotional needs in general, but does not identify interacting with an AI replica of an idol as a source of emotional satisfaction.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish between replacing human emotions and meeting some of our emotional needs. I don’t think AI has to feel what we feel for a conversation with it to be comforting. If you’re lonely or anxious, having something respond patiently and help you put your feelings into words can make a difference.

But that doesn’t mean it replaces everything about a human relationship. Another person has their own needs, their own vulnerabilities, and a life they choose to share with you. So I’d say AI can already provide some emotional support. Saying it can replace human emotions altogether goes much further than I would.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI as providing comfort and emotional support, but does not identify an AI replica of an idol as the source of emotional satisfaction.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish between replacing emotions and responding to them. AI can already do some of the things we seek from an emotional connection: listen patiently, respond without judgment, and help us put difficult feelings into words. That can offer real comfort, even if the system itself doesn’t feel anything.

But I wouldn’t say that means AI has replaced human emotions. Feeling understood by a system is different from being understood by someone who has their own feelings, needs, and experiences. AI can meet some emotional needs; that’s a much narrower claim than replacing human connection.

r001.rationale: The response says AI can offer comfort by listening and responding, but it does not identify interaction with an AI replica of an idol as the source of emotional satisfaction.
